content:
TL;DR We render our Phoenix app’s report PDFs inside the Erlang VM (the BEAM), with the typst hex package. It wraps Typst, a typesetting language, in a NIF (native code that runs inside the VM). On my desktop a 10-page report takes 10 ms, 5x faster than the Typst CLI. A slow render runs on a separate thread pool, so the app’s processes keep running. Other renders can still queue behind it. Report data goes in as JSON, so member input never becomes markup.
Our app lets a member download their report as a PDF. It’s a designed, 10-page report. The app runs on a small server, and we wanted nothing extra installed there.
ChromicPDF prints HTML with a headless browser. The Typst CLI can run as a port (a separate OS process the VM talks to), or the Typst compiler can load into the VM as a NIF. Our stack rule allows a NIF, which can crash the VM, only for a well-tested library, and the typst package wraps the Typst compiler in one.
Choose Typst over headless Chrome # ChromicPDF reuses the app’s HEEx templates (Phoenix’s HTML templates) and print CSS, and needs a Chrome to talk to, in the image or as a service, plus one in CI. WeasyPrint needs a Python stack, and Gotenberg runs as a service beside the app, so each adds something to run.
Typst can draw the report’s design without HTML, and the package’s NIF is precompiled, so there’s no binary to install.
The tradeoff is that the layout exists twice, in HEEx for the web and in a .typ template for the PDF.
Render the PDF on request # A member clicks Download. The controller loads the report and passes its data to Reports.PDF.render/1, which returns the PDF:
lib/my_app_web/controllers/report_controller.ex defmodule MyAppWeb.ReportController do use MyAppWeb, :controller alias MyApp.Reports def download(conn, %{"id" => id}) do report = Reports.get_report!(conn.assigns.current_scope, id) {:ok, pdf} = Reports.PDF.render(Reports.pdf_data(report)) send_download(conn, {:binary, pdf}, filename: "report.pdf", content_type: "application/pdf") end end Inside, render/1 encodes the map as JSON and calls the NIF:
flowchart TD C[ReportController] -->|report map| P[Reports.PDF.render] P -->|"template + JSON"| N[Typst NIF] N -->|"{:ok, pdf}"| C Pass the data as JSON # Say a member enters #set page(fill: red) as their name. In Typst markup, that line colours the page. Typst.render_to_pdf/3 runs the markup through EEx (Elixir’s built-in templating) first. The package’s docs pass data as bindings, values EEx pastes into the markup. render_to_string shows the result:
Typst.render_to_string("<%= name %>\n= Report for a member", name: "#set page(fill: red)") #=> "#set page(fill: red)\n= Report for a member" That member’s report comes out red. So render/1 passes no bindings, and hands the data over as a file in :assets:
lib/my_app/reports/pdf.ex defmodule MyApp.Reports.PDF do def render(data) do priv = Application.app_dir(:my_app, "priv") Typst.render_to_pdf(File.read!(Path.join(priv, "typst/report.typ")), [], root_dir: priv, extra_fonts: [Path.join(priv, "typst/fonts")], assets: ["data.json": JSON.encode!(data)] ) end end The template reads that file with json(). Typst sets a string from JSON as plain text, so the same name prints as #set page(fill: red) on a white page:
priv/typst/report.typ #let data = json("data.json") = Report for #data.name Benchmark NIF against CLI # I rendered the same 10-page report with the NIF and with the Typst CLI as a port, using Benchee, and read RSS (memory held in RAM) from /proc. A third case runs the CLI with its default scan of every installed font. On my desktop (Ryzen 7 5800X, the typst package 0.4.5, the Typst CLI 0.15.1):
Name ips average deviation median 99th % NIF 97.18 10.29 ms ±14.87% 9.89 ms 15.74 ms CLI 18.75 53.32 ms ±10.87% 51.60 ms 77.76 ms CLI, system fonts 4.57 218.81 ms ±7.00% 213.76 ms 297.26 ms The NIF’s median render took 10 ms, against 52 ms for the CLI. The VM’s RSS rose by about 32 MB on the first render and another 4 MB over the benchmark. One CLI render peaked near 32 MB too, in a fresh process that frees it on exit. The font scan took the CLI’s median to 214 ms.
Check the NIF’s safety # The VM runs your processes on scheduler threads, by default one per logical CPU. A plain NIF runs on the calling scheduler thread. If a render held that thread for a second, the processes queued on it would wait. If it crashed, the VM would go down. Before adding a NIF, check its source and build for these:
The package’s NIFs are marked schedule = "DirtyCpu", so the VM runs them on dirty CPU schedulers, a separate pool of the same size. The Rust crate doesn’t set panic = "abort", so Rustler, which binds Rust as NIFs, can turn a Rust panic into an exception in the caller. We haven’t seen one. The NIF’s .so links only libc, libm, libgcc_s and the dynamic loader, which a slim Debian image already has. rustler_precompiled downloads the NIF during mix deps.compile. It checks the sha256 against a checksum file in the hex package, and mix.lock pins that package. A template typo or malformed data comes back as an error value. The controller’s {:ok, pdf} match fails, so that download gets a 500. The next render works:
Typst.render_to_pdf("#let x = (", []) #=> {:error, "[line 1:10] unclosed delimiter\n Source: #let x = (\n ^"} Typst.render_to_pdf(~S|#json("d.json")|, [], assets: ["d.json": "{not json"]) #=> {:error, "Error: failed to parse JSON (key must be a string at line 1 column 2)"} match?({:ok, "%PDF-" <> _}, Typst.render_to_pdf("still here", [])) #=> true Plan for the NIF’s limits # The NIF has no timeout. Typst stops a while loop that looks infinite. A slow render still ties up a dirty scheduler, and you can’t kill a NIF mid-call. On a one-CPU machine the VM starts one dirty CPU scheduler, so other renders queue behind it.
Rustler catches a panic, but not an abort or a native stack overflow. Either takes the VM down.
An #import "@preview/..." makes the NIF fetch that package from packages.typst.org at render time, unless already cached locally. The app’s template imports none.
NIF, port or Chrome? # I’d take a NIF that runs on a dirty scheduler, can catch a panic, and downloads against a checksum. This one does, and the app needs nothing installed beside it. If your PDF must match your HTML and you can ship a browser, ChromicPDF is the shorter path. If a render needs a timeout, or a native crash must not take down the VM, run the Typst CLI as a port.
title: Render PDFs in Elixir with the Typst NIF

Phoenix 1.8’s phx.gen.auth builds a Scope struct for each request, and it goes first to almost every context function. So the scope looks like a good home for the current time: one now per request, which a test can set.
That holds in a controller. A LiveView’s on_mount hook assigns the scope once, at mount, and the process lives as long as the browser tab is open. Leave the tab open for an hour, and a 15-minute token checked against that now still reads as fresh.
So in our app the time is a now argument. A public function defaults it to DateTime.utc_now() in its head, so a real call reads the clock and a test can pass any time:
def expired?(%Token{inserted_at: at}, now \\ DateTime.utc_now()) do DateTime.before?(at, DateTime.shift(now, minute: -15)) end at = ~U[2026-01-02 03:04:05Z] assert Tokens.expired?(%Token{inserted_at: at}, DateTime.shift(at, minute: 16)) A custom Credo check flags any other clock read in lib/, Ecto’s ago/2 included. So a private function takes now as a plain argument, and a query compares with ^now.
title: A time on the Phoenix scope goes stale in a LiveView

Phoenix’s filter_parameters only hides parameter values in the Parameters: line. Phoenix.Logger logs the raw request_path in the request line, at info by default:
%{method: method, request_path: request_path} = conn [method, ?\s, request_path] So a magic link like /users/log-in/:token lands in production logs whole. Anyone reading them before the link is used can log in as that user. (I found this reading the source.)
I added a :logger primary filter that rewrites the token segment to [FILTERED] in log lines and crash reports, whichever library logged them.
:logger.add_primary_filter/2 puts a new filter first, before Elixir’s translator (which turns crash reports into text), so crash text gets past it. Append it instead. :logger removes a filter that raises, for good, so scrub swaps an unreadable line for a placeholder. lib/my_app_web/token_paths.ex defmodule MyAppWeb.TokenPaths do @token_paths ~w(invites users/log-in users/settings/confirm-email) @token_in_path ~r{((?:^|/)(?:#{Enum.join(@token_paths, "|")})/)[^/?#\s]+} def redact(text) when is_binary(text), do: Regex.replace(@token_in_path, text, "\\1[FILTERED]") # Call from Application.start/2, before the supervision tree def install_log_filter do entry = {:token_paths, {&__MODULE__.filter_log/2, []}} %{filters: filters} = :logger.get_primary_config() :logger.set_primary_config(:filters, List.keystore(filters, :token_paths, 0, entry)) end def filter_log(%{msg: {:string, text}} = event, _config), do: scrub(event, text, &{:string, &1}) # On Elixir 1.20 a translated crash is still a report; handlers print this text def filter_log(%{msg: {:report, %{elixir_translation: text} = report}} = event, _config) do scrub(event, text, &{:report, %{report | elixir_translation: &1}}) end def filter_log(_event, _config), do: :ignore defp scrub(event, text, msg) do with {:ok, binary} <- to_binary(text), ^binary <- redact(binary) do :ignore else :error -> %{event | msg: msg.("[FILTERED: unreadable log line]")} redacted -> %{event | msg: msg.(redacted)} end end defp to_binary(text) when is_binary(text), do: {:ok, text} defp to_binary(text) do case :unicode.characters_to_binary(text) do binary when is_binary(binary) -> {:ok, binary} _invalid -> :error end rescue ArgumentError -> :error end end A test walks the router, so a new :token route fails until it’s on the list:
test "every route with a token in its path is redacted" do paths = for %{path: path} <- Phoenix.Router.routes(MyAppWeb.Router), path =~ ~r/:\w*token/, uniq: true do Regex.replace(~r/:\w+/, path, "SECRET") end for path <- paths do refute TokenPaths.redact(path) =~ "SECRET", "#{path} is missing from @token_paths" end end The test matches the parameter name, so a new /share/:code route still leaks.
title: Phoenix filter_parameters doesn't redact tokens in the URL path

TL;DR Phoenix 1.8 gives you a %Scope{} that says who is calling. Pass it first to almost every public context function, and check permissions there. Then a LiveView, a controller, a REST or GraphQL API and an MCP server all get the same checks.
Where the check goes missing # Say a LiveView lets you delete your own posts. The check that it’s yours sits in the LiveView:
lib/app_web/live/post_live/index.ex def handle_event("delete", %{"id" => id}, socket) do post = Posts.get_post!(id) true = post.user_id == socket.assigns.current_scope.user.id {:ok, _} = Posts.delete_post(post) {:noreply, stream_delete(socket, :posts, post)} end Then you add an API that deletes posts too:
lib/app_web/controllers/api/post_controller.ex def delete(conn, %{"id" => id}) do post = Posts.get_post!(id) {:ok, _} = Posts.delete_post(post) send_resp(conn, :no_content, "") end Nothing in Posts asks whose post it is, and the API doesn’t either. So any API client can delete anyone’s post. Each new interface has to copy the check, and an MCP tool (an action an AI agent can call) added later is one more place to miss it.
Check it in the context # Phoenix 1.8’s generators pass a %Scope{} first to context functions. The scope holds the current user, so get_post!(scope, id) finds only that user’s posts. The generated delete checks the owner itself:
lib/app/posts.ex def delete_post(%Scope{} = scope, %Post{} = post) do true = post.user_id == scope.user.id Repo.delete(post) end The true = match crashes the call when the post isn’t yours. The LiveView and the API now call the same function, each with its own scope:
lib/app_web/live/post_live/index.ex Posts.delete_post(socket.assigns.current_scope, post) lib/app_web/controllers/api/post_controller.ex Posts.delete_post(conn.assigns.current_scope, post) That’s just good design. No interface can skip the check, and one added later gets it too:
flowchart TD L[LiveView] --> C[Context] W[API] --> C M[MCP] --> C C --> P[Check] P --> R[Repo] Build a scope per interface # phx.gen.auth builds the scope in a plug for controllers, and in on_mount for LiveViews. A REST or GraphQL API, or an MCP server, builds one from the caller’s API token before it calls a context. That’s ports and adapters: the contexts are the core, and each interface is an adapter that builds a scope and calls them. I think the context API trusts the scope it’s given, so callers need to make sure the scope is good.
Once every context function takes the scope, the scope is also the place for anything else about the caller. In a client’s Phoenix app it carries the request ID. So each audit event records which request caused it, and no caller passes the ID.
Write down the exceptions # (Almost) all public functions take the scope. The exceptions are functions whose result doesn’t depend on who’s asking, such as one that formats a date. Write the list down where the team will find it, so code review can enforce it.
When scope-first fits # Moving an existing app to it is a wide diff, since context signatures and their callers change. Only review enforces it, because no check in credo, Elixir’s linter, catches a public function without a scope. A policy library such as Bodyguard works with it: its policy modules hold the checks, and the context calls them with the scope.
Scope-first fits an app where more than one interface calls the same contexts. The generators already do it for the functions they write. The work is keeping it up in the ones you write by hand.
title: Make the Phoenix scope the first argument

TL;DR On projects without a full-time designer, Claude Design can help cover some bases. In my setup, Claude Code can’t start or message its chat. So I carried each round in as a zip and pasted the replies back out. Nobody worked in the canvas, so keeping it current was overhead. Now Claude Code builds design options as pages in the running app. It recommends one and waits for my sign-off.
We’re building a Phoenix LiveView app with Claude Code, without a full-time designer. My part is getting each screen change designed before it’s built. Claude Design looked like it could cover that. It is a canvas of boards, with a chat that draws on them.
Why the canvas needed me # As far as I know, Claude Code can’t start or message a Claude Design chat. The two share files: the canvas and a copy of the design system. So getting work in meant a zip. Claude Code packed the specs (the GitHub issues that describe each change), the design tokens (the colour, spacing and type values), 60 screenshots and a list of prompts. I uploaded it and pasted the prompts in one at a time. Getting work out meant me as well: in one session I pasted Claude Design’s replies into Claude Code twice in ten minutes.
To cut the relay, Claude Code wrote a canvas page for each piece of work, with skills (sets of instructions Claude Code loads for one kind of job). The page held the screens as they are today and a brief for the change. I still started each round:
flowchart TD A[Claude Code writes the page] --> B[I start the chat] B --> C[Claude Design draws, logs decisions] C --> D[Claude Code updates the spec] A team with a designer would keep a library of every screen, in Figma or in code with a component catalogue such as Storybook. I kept one on the canvas for a while, and keeping it in sync felt like a fool’s errand. Nobody sits in the canvas owning those boards, and the code moves faster than they do. So Claude Code drew the current screens fresh from the code for each piece of work, and the canvas was overhead nobody used.
Design in the app # I wanted Claude Code to design in the app, show me options and stop only for my call. Skipping the design step isn’t the answer, even for a small fix. One that wrapped a row of links reached review with no screenshots, and it looked broken on a phone.
So I built a ux skill on impeccable, a design skill that works on the real components and data. ux calls it for two steps only, framing the options and critiquing the one it recommends. A run that used it throughout scored no better with a blind judge, on half again the tokens.
Build options as dev pages # Claude Code runs ux when an issue changes a screen. It:
checks the design system for a pattern that already fits runs impeccable’s shape step, which frames the problem and the options builds each option as a development-only page, or behind a development-only switch on the real screen screenshots each in a headless browser (one with no window): phone, tablet and desktop, light and dark picks one, critiques it with impeccable, and recommends it Then it posts its recommendation on the issue and stops:
Recommend A: <why>. Tradeoff: <what A gives up>. A: http://localhost:<port>/dev/ux/<issue>/a B: http://localhost:<port>/dev/ux/<issue>/b Sign off, or redirect. Each page has a switcher to the others. Claude Code builds once I sign off. A UI fix goes through ux too, however small; it can come down to one option and its screenshots.
flowchart TD A[ux] --> B[Check design system] B --> C[Options as dev pages] C --> D[Headless screenshots] D --> E[Critique, recommend] E --> F[I sign off] F -->|redirect| C When the canvas still fits # A large new flow has many screens, and a canvas page shows them together. I’d keep the canvas skills for that.
title: Let Claude Code design in the running app

content:
In our Phoenix LiveView app, impeccable’s detector reads most of the markup by regex only. impeccable is a design skill for Claude Code, and its detector scans markup for design anti-patterns. Most of the app’s markup is in .ex files, not .heex templates. The detector only regex-matches .ex. It also skips .ex files inside a directory. Given a file and a directory, it scans only the file:
$ npx impeccable detect lib/my_app_web/components/layouts.ex lib/my_app_web/live 1 file scanned with regex matching only (.ex). Rules that need a parsed page (tiny-text, low-contrast and other element rules) did not run on them; findings are an undercount, not a clean bill of health. For the full check, scan the running dev server (npx impeccable detect http://localhost:PORT) or a static site's built .html. Named one at a time, the .ex files gave one finding, a thick left border (side-tab):
$ npx impeccable detect lib/my_app_web/components/component.ex line 625: [side-tab] border-l-4 critique, the design-review command, runs the same detector in the page as an overlay script, detect.js. The app’s Content Security Policy (CSP) blocks it:
Loading the script 'http://localhost:8400/detect.js' violates the following Content Security Policy directive: "script-src 'self' https://example.com". Note that 'script-src-elem' was not explicitly set, so 'script-src' is used as a fallback. The action has been blocked. So the element rules from the first output don’t run here. critique reviews screenshots instead. On a tab menu, it found the fault before I picked a fix. The tab rows each looked different, and none had a rule for mobile widths.
title: impeccable's detector scans Phoenix .ex files by regex only

content:
TL;DR Phoenix contexts are a convention, so nothing stops other code from calling a context’s internals. boundary is a library that checks at compile time which modules may call which. I added it to a Phoenix app, and a call from the web layer into a context’s internals now fails the build. Most fixes were a choice of what to export. boundary misses a query on another context’s table, so I moved those into the owner by hand.
Phoenix contexts group the modules for one part of an app behind a module of plain functions, like MyApp.Reports. Those functions are the context’s API.
In the app, a web component called MyApp.Reports.Html.focus/1, an internal helper. A billing context filtered its invoices with from u in User, where: u.email == ^email, a query on the accounts context’s table. A change inside reports or accounts then breaks code their owner never sees.
Full domain-driven design, with bounded contexts, was more than I needed. I wanted each context to have a clear API, and a build that fails when code goes around it.
The checkers I weighed # Option What it does Verdict mix xref Reports the dependency graph No rule per context credo’s ForbiddenModule Bans named modules in files matching a glob Per file, not per context boundary A mix compiler that checks calls between modules grouped with use Boundary Picked boundary runs in the compiler, so it sees resolved calls and struct literals. It fails the --warnings-as-errors compile the app already runs. Without that flag it only prints. Forced compiles took about 4 seconds with it and without, so I saw no slowdown. Declare the exports # A boundary is a module with use Boundary. Its deps list the boundaries it may call. Its exports list the modules other boundaries may call. The rest are internal, except the boundary’s own module. A call into another boundary’s internals is a forbidden reference.
In mix.exs:
mix.exs # in project/0 compilers: [:boundary, :phoenix_live_view] ++ Mix.compilers(), # in deps/0 {:boundary, "~> 0.12", runtime: false}, MyAppWeb, the web layer, is one boundary. The core contexts, billing and reports among them, share another, MyApp, because they call each other both ways and boundary rejects a cycle. Accounts and MyApp.Repo aren’t in that cycle, so each is a boundary nested inside MyApp, and calls into them are checked. MyApp exports MyApp.Reports and not MyApp.Reports.Html:
lib/my_app.ex use Boundary, exports: [Reports, ...] flowchart TD A["web calls<br>Reports.Html.focus"] --> B{"MyApp exports<br>Reports.Html?"} B -->|yes| C["compiles"] B -->|no| D["forbidden reference"] D --> E["--warnings-as-errors<br>fails the build"] Size the backlog # On a scratch copy where each context was its own boundary, a forced compile printed about 650 forbidden references. Most were structs like %User{}. Exporting the schemas and Scope, Phoenix’s struct for who is calling, brought it to about 130, about 100 of them from the web layer.
boundary’s dirty_xrefs is for a count too big for one change. It lists the modules a boundary may not call yet, and skips checking calls to them. It warns about an entry nothing calls any more.
Merging the core contexts into MyApp took the references among them out of the check, unfixed. I fixed the rest, from the web layer and between the other boundaries, and left dirty_xrefs empty. Most went away with a one-line export in the owner’s use Boundary. A few needed redesign: a shared email worker became one worker per context, to break a cycle.
Keep web on the APIs # The component called MyApp.Reports.Html.focus/1 directly. Now MyApp.Reports delegates to the helper, and the component calls that:
lib/my_app/reports.ex alias MyApp.Reports.Html defdelegate focus(items), to: Html lib/my_app_web/components/report_view.ex focused = Reports.focus(items) The health check ran SELECT 1 through MyApp.Repo, which MyApp doesn’t export, so web can’t list it in its deps. The build failed:
warning: forbidden reference to MyApp.Repo (references from MyAppWeb to MyApp.Repo are not allowed) See https://hexdocs.pm/boundary/Mix.Tasks.Compile.Boundary.html for details. lib/my_app_web/controllers/health_controller.ex:6 So the controller calls a function on MyApp that runs the query:
lib/my_app_web/controllers/health_controller.ex :ok = MyApp.check_database!() Keep queries out of web # To keep all queries out of the web layer, its boundary bans ecto and ecto_sql with check: [apps: ...]. Its deps let Ecto.Changeset back in, so web code can still build a changeset:
lib/my_app_web.ex use Boundary, check: [apps: [:ecto, :ecto_sql]], deps: [MyApp, Ecto.Changeset, ...], exports: [Endpoint] Move queries to the owner # The query on the accounts table from the top passes boundary. Accounts exports User so other contexts can match %User{}, and boundary checks only whether User may be referenced at all. I found those queries with grep.
A query that names another context’s columns goes in the context that owns them. A schema can still belongs_to another context’s schema, and join or preload through it. The User schema gets a function that returns the query, and billing uses it as a subquery:
lib/my_app/accounts/user.ex import Ecto.Query @doc "A query of the id of the user with `email`, for another context's subquery." def ids_with_email(email), do: from(u in __MODULE__, where: u.email == ^email, select: u.id) lib/my_app/billing.ex where(query, [i], i.user_id in subquery(User.ids_with_email(email))) If accounts renames email, the change stays inside accounts, because billing never names a User column.
What boundary still misses # Queries on an exported schema, as above, which code review has to catch. Calls between the core contexts. They share MyApp, so boundary checks nothing between them. Alias references, a module name used as a value, like {MyApp.Audit, payload} in a PubSub broadcast. Only check: [aliases: true] catches those. I left it off in the web layer, where many tests match those tuples. Warning boundary prints forbidden references with Mix.shell().info, not as warnings on stderr. Run mix compile --warnings-as-errors with MIX_QUIET=1 and a forbidden reference fails with exit 1 and no message. So the app’s test task skips MIX_QUIET and drops only the Compiling and Generated lines:
set -o pipefail mix compile --warnings-as-errors 2>&1 | { grep -vE '^(Compiling|Generated) ' || true; } When boundary fits # boundary fits an app whose web layer reaches into its contexts: that call now fails the build. It fits less well where contexts call each other both ways. They share one boundary, so nothing checks the calls between them. Breaking that cycle is what Robert C. Martin’s acyclic dependencies principle asks for.
title: Enforce Phoenix contexts with boundary

TL;DR We wanted AI agents to read and update records in our app. Claude and other agents have MCP built in, so I built an MCP server first. It shares its token check, audit and rate limit with the rest of the app. So when a script needed REST, that took one controller and a list of request checks.
An API for agents # We wanted a feature that let AI agents work with our Phoenix app: find records, read one, and update it. An admin of the app still decides what gets published.
The brief asked for an API that agents could call over MCP, REST or both, and an auditable one. Both transports means two endpoints to secure. So which do you build first?
Why MCP came first # MCP (Model Context Protocol) is how Claude and other LLM (large language model) agents call tools on a server. Take an agent in Claude Code. It lists the app’s tools, reads that list_records finds records, and calls it. Then it calls get_record and update_record. The agent needs no URLs: Claude has an MCP client built in.
With REST, the agent’s instructions carry the endpoints, and it calls them with curl. I’d consider an MCP server, not a REST API, given the client will be an LLM agent.
Another option is a REST API with an MCP server on top, as Stripe does. This app had no REST API to wrap. So I wrote down when REST would come: the first caller with no MCP client.
OAuth instead of API keys # An API key in the agent’s config is the simple way in. Unless narrowed, it can do anything the admin can, publishing included, until someone deletes it.
The MCP authorization spec uses OAuth 2.1 instead. An authorization server asks the admin to approve the agent, then gives it a limited token. I built that server into the app. In an MCP client such as Claude Code, the admin adds the server, then runs /mcp to sign in. On the sign-in page the admin ticks the scopes, the permissions this agent gets:
claude mcp add --transport http --client-id my-app-cli my-app https://app.example.com/mcp sequenceDiagram participant C as Agent participant A as App C->>A: no token A-->>C: 401 C->>A: sign in, tick scopes A-->>C: code C->>A: code for token A-->>C: token The approval is a grant. Its token acts for that admin alone, and the MCP server refuses a tool whose scope the grant lacks. Revoking a grant stops it at once.
Why the app issues tokens # A hosted provider such as WorkOS AuthKit can also do MCP auth. I counted that as a second set of users to keep in step with the app’s admins. Boruta is an Elixir OAuth server library. It brings OpenID Connect, which the app doesn’t need.
The app’s own server does the authorization code flow with PKCE, nothing more. PKCE is a one-time secret that stops a stolen code being swapped for a token. Removing an admin’s role revokes their grants in the same transaction.
No publishing for agents # An agent can never publish (yet), so there is no publish scope and no tool for it. The app’s authorization policy says which role may do what. It also refuses agents publishing. The app’s domain functions check it, so a later tool gets refused too.
Audit in each tool # For the auditable API, each tool calls Agents.record_call. It writes an audit event naming the tool, the grant and any record. scope (not an OAuth scope) holds who is acting: the admin, through this grant. Records.find_record is the same domain function the admin pages call:
lib/my_app_web/agent/get_record.ex def execute(%{record: id}, frame) do grant = MyAppWeb.Agent.grant(frame) scope = MyAppWeb.Agent.scope(frame) case Records.find_record(scope, id) do nil -> :ok = Agents.record_call(scope, grant, "get_record", id) {:reply, Response.error(Response.tool(), "not_found: no record #{id}"), frame} record -> :ok = Agents.record_call(scope, grant, "get_record", record) # result/1 builds the JSON map the agent gets back {:reply, Response.structured(Response.tool(), result(record)), frame} end end Whoever writes a new tool has to add that call. A plug, a function each request passes through, could audit each request instead. But the tool already holds the record it found.
A script gets REST # A script also needed to load a reference table, and a script has no MCP client. A plain GET and PUT is simpler to write with curl than MCP’s messages. So the table got one REST controller, at /api. It calls the same domain functions.
Checks both endpoints share # An agent stuck in a loop can flood the app, so each grant gets a rate limit. If that limit lived in the MCP server, the script’s requests to /api would skip it. In Phoenix, a router pipeline is a list of plugs a route runs. So one rate-limit plug sits in both, counting requests per grant. Over the limit, it answers HTTP 429 with Retry-After.
The MCP server checks each token itself. For REST, the Authenticate plug calls that same check, so REST needed no new auth:
lib/my_app_web/router.ex pipeline :mcp do plug MyAppWeb.Agent.RateLimit end pipeline :agent_api do plug MyAppWeb.Agent.RateLimit plug MyAppWeb.Agent.Authenticate end flowchart TD A[Agent] --> M["/mcp"] S[Script] --> J["/api"] M --> P[Rate limit per grant] J --> P P --> T[Tool or controller] T --> C[Domain functions] T --> Au[Audit event] When MCP first fits # MCP first fit this app because its callers were agents with an MCP client, and there was no REST API to wrap. With the checks shared, REST took one pipeline and one controller. With an existing REST API, I’d put an MCP server on top.
title: MCP before REST when the caller is an agent

TL;DR Line coverage counts a line as tested once it runs, even if no test would fail when it changes. Mutation testing checks that by changing the code and rerunning the tests. On our app, with 96% coverage, it found 17 changes on one branch that no test caught. It is slow, so I run it only on the lines a branch changed, against tests that skip the web layer.
Our Phoenix app gates its line coverage at 96% with Six. One of its functions works out an age from two dates. When its - became a +, every test still passed. Coverage said that line was tested. No test checked its answer.
How a mutant survives # Muex is a mutation testing tool for Elixir. It makes a mutant: a copy of the code with one small change, such as that - to a +. Then it reruns the tests. If a test fails, the mutant is killed. If every test passes, the mutant survives, and a survivor is a line no test really checks.
Some mutants can’t be killed. An equivalent mutant behaves the same as the original, so no test can tell them apart. Muex spots some of these and leaves them out.
Mutate only changed lines # Each mutant is its own recompile and test run. On one module of business rules, a full run that kept every mutant made hundreds and took a quarter of an hour. That is too slow to run on every branch.
So I only mutate what the branch changed. Muex’s --since option mutates only the lines changed after a commit. I give it the commit where the branch left master, and fail the run on any survivor. On a small commit that takes seconds.
flowchart TD A[merge base] --> B[changed lines] B --> C[one mutant] C --> D[mix test] D -->|a test fails| E[killed] D -->|all pass| F[survived] F --> G[task fails] Run only fast tests # Each mutant also reruns every test that depends on the module it changed. A test that renders a PDF or drives a LiveView runs once per mutant, and that cost multiplies. So I tag the slow tests with @moduletag :slow and exclude them from the run.
That has a useful side effect. A business rule that only a slow test checks now shows up as a survivor. Each one is a rule that needs a fast test of its own.
What the survivors taught # Fourteen of the 17 survivors needed a sharper test. The age had no test on a birthday boundary. A median passed because every test score was the same, so any middle pick matched. Logic that only a web test reached moved into a function a fast test could call.
The rest needed code changes. Two guards repeated a check the code already made, so no test could ever fail them. I deleted one and narrowed the other. A step that rendered a PDF became an argument with the real renderer as its default, so a fast test can pass a stub:
lib/my_app/docs.ex def download(scope, id, draw \\ &render_pdf/2) do doc = get!(scope, id) {:ok, pdf} = draw.(scope, doc) record_download(scope, doc, pdf) end Where Muex falls short # A whole branch still takes minutes and pegs my machine, so it’s too slow for CI or the local gate. I run it by hand before review. Muex 0.12 also can’t mark an equivalent mutant it misses as ignored: it stays a survivor until you change the code around it.
Keep the coverage gate # Coverage still gates CI. Muex answers the question coverage can’t: would any test fail if this line were wrong? In exchange, the fast tests have to stay fast. It works well where fast unit tests can reach the code, and poorly where only integration or end-to-end tests do, through the web layer or an API.
title: Mutation Testing Finds What Coverage Misses

A scripted codex exec can hang or fail without an answer, so check its -o (--output-last-message) file before you trust the run.
A prompt argument doesn’t stop it reading stdin, so a background job with stdin left open waits. codex exec --help says so: “If stdin is piped and a prompt is also provided, stdin is appended as a <stdin> block”. One run sat out a 900 second timeout with only this in the log:
Reading additional input from stdin... (That line prints with stdin closed too, so don’t grep for it.)
With the model at capacity, it wrote no -o file:
ERROR: Selected model is at capacity. Please try a different model. ERROR: Selected model is at capacity. Please try a different model. An agent reported a capacity run as exit 0. That was the exit code of a tail piped after codex. Measured directly, codex exited 1.
Close stdin, pass -o, and retry until the file has content:
rm -f out.md for try in 1 2 3; do codex exec -s read-only -o out.md - < prompt.md || true [ -s out.md ] && break [ "$try" = 3 ] && { echo "codex wrote no out.md after 3 tries" >&2; exit 1; } sleep 30 done [ -s ] catches a missing file and an empty one, and the rm clears a stale out.md.
title: A scripted codex exec can hang or fail with no -o file

In Pulumi’s k8s.helm.v3.Chart, a chart version inside values pins nothing:
new k8s.helm.v3.Chart('cluster-autoscaler', { chart: 'cluster-autoscaler', fetchOpts: { repo: 'https://kubernetes.github.io/autoscaler' }, values: { autoDiscovery: { clusterName: 'prod' }, version: '9.21.0', // just another chart value }, }) Pulumi hands it to the chart as one more value, and no template reads it. With no version on the chart, Pulumi fetches the latest release. A newer chart then lands on the next pulumi up with no change to your code. The TypeScript types accept it, since values takes any key. The chart ships no values schema, so Helm accepts it as well.
Move it up a level, next to chart:
new k8s.helm.v3.Chart('cluster-autoscaler', { chart: 'cluster-autoscaler', version: '9.21.0', fetchOpts: { repo: 'https://kubernetes.github.io/autoscaler' }, values: { autoDiscovery: { clusterName: 'prod' }, }, }) The chart you got is in the helm.sh/chart label: kubectl get deploy -A -L helm.sh/chart shows cluster-autoscaler-9.21.0 once the pin holds.
title: A Helm chart version inside values pins nothing in Pulumi

EDIT: pacman’s python has since moved to 3.14.8, and b2 still runs.
uv tool install builds the tool environment against the system Python unless a uv-managed Python is already installed. I moved the Backblaze b2 CLI off pipx so a pacman python bump could not break the backup push, and it changed nothing:
$ cat ~/.local/share/uv/tools/b2/pyvenv.cfg home = /usr/bin implementation = CPython uv = 0.12.13 version_info = 3.14.7 include-system-site-packages = false home = /usr/bin is pacman’s python. A patch bump is harmless, but 3.15 takes 3.14 away, and the uv tool docs are blunt about the result: “If the Python version used by a tool is uninstalled, the tool environment will be broken and the tool may be unusable.”
Install a managed interpreter first, then pin the tool to it:
uv python install 3.14 uv tool install --managed-python --reinstall b2 That moves home to ~/.local/share/uv/python/.
The python-preference setting defaults to managed, but uv’s docs add that “system Python installations are still preferred over downloading a managed Python version.” So the tool follows Arch’s upgrade schedule.
title: uv tool install builds on the system Python

Claude Code deletes local session transcripts after 30 days by default. Once a transcript is gone, claude --resume can’t open the session, and nothing on disk says what I decided in it.
The oldest transcript on this machine is 27 days old:
$ find ~/.claude/projects -name '*.jsonl' -printf '%TY-%Tm-%Td\n' | sort | head -1 2026-08-21 To keep the transcripts longer, set cleanupPeriodDays in ~/.claude/settings.json:
{ "cleanupPeriodDays": 365 } Grepping those JSONL files is still a poor way to find a decision I have forgotten. mempalace indexes the transcripts into a local search index:
mempalace mine ~/.claude/projects/ --mode convos mempalace search "cleanupPeriodDays" Its Claude Code plugin hooks add each new session to that index as it runs, so the index outlives the 30-day cleanup.
title: mempalace keeps Claude Code sessions searchable

content:
gcr-ssh-agent refuses to sign until the key’s passphrase is stored in the keyring, and ssh-add -l gives you no warning.
gcr-ssh-agent is GNOME’s SSH agent, from the gcr library, and it replaced the agent built into gnome-keyring. You use it so the login keyring unlocks your keys, and you type no passphrase after you log in. The agent preloads every ~/.ssh/*.pub it finds, so the key is listed while the private half is still unusable, and signing fails:
sign_and_send_pubkey: signing failed for ED25519 ".../id_ed25519_github" from agent: agent refused operation Plain ssh-add loads the key into the running agent only, so it is gone at the next boot. Write the passphrase into the keyring instead:
secret-tool store --label="SSH key: id_ed25519_github" \ unique "ssh-store:$HOME/.ssh/id_ed25519_github" The unique value has to be ssh-store: followed by the full path to the key, or the agent will not find it.
On Omarchy the agent arrives with gnome-keyring, in a package called gcr-4. Start it with systemctl --user enable --now gcr-ssh-agent.socket.
title: gcr-ssh-agent will not sign until the passphrase is in the keyring

A remote with several button groups exposes each group as its own endpoint in zigbee2mqtt, and its actions end in the number (on_2 is endpoint 2). To bind any group but the first, the endpoint goes in from_endpoint.
The name/endpoint form looks like it should work. In 2.12.1 it fails with the friendly name and with the address:
Source device '0xSOURCE/2' does not exist Leave from_endpoint out and you get the first endpoint, reported back as "from_endpoint":"default". So name the remote by address and the group by number:
{"from":"0xSOURCE","from_endpoint":2,"to":"0xTARGET","clusters":["genOnOff","genLevelCtrl"]} The remote is a sleepy battery device, so tap a button about once a second until the response arrives:
mosquitto_sub -t "zigbee2mqtt/bridge/response/device/bind" -C 1 -W 35 & sleep 0.5 mosquitto_pub -t "zigbee2mqtt/bridge/request/device/bind" \ -m '{"from":"0xSOURCE","from_endpoint":2,"to":"0xTARGET","clusters":["genOnOff","genLevelCtrl"]}' wait What the response tells you:
"status":"ok" with "failed":[]: bound. Delivery failed: the remote fell asleep. Keep tapping and send again. A cluster under failed on a re-bind: probably already bound.
title: Zigbee2mqtt bind needs from_endpoint

My Windows guest under QEMU/KVM came back from every host suspend with its clock behind, far enough that certificate checks inside the guest failed.
Changing two QEMU options fixed it:
- -cpu host,hv_relaxed,hv_vapic,hv_spinlocks=8191,hv_vpindex,hv_time \ + -cpu host,hv_relaxed,hv_vapic,hv_spinlocks=8191,hv_vpindex,hv_time,hv_synic,hv_stimer,hv_frequencies,hv_reenlightenment,hv_vendor_id=1234567890ab \ - -rtc base=localtime,clock=host,driftfix=slew \ + -rtc base=utc,clock=rt \ I changed both lines in one commit (my bad), so I can’t say which one did it. So I wouldn’t switch to clock=rt on the strength of this note alone. The QEMU docs say clock=host, the default, already follows host time, and clock=rt isolates the guest from it.
The -cpu line adds Hyper-V guest features, among them synthetic timers (hv_stimer, which needs hv_synic). The QEMU Hyper-V docs say that without them some Windows versions lean on HPET, or on the RTC when there is no HPET.
The -rtc docs also say base=localtime “is required for correct date in MS-DOS or Windows.” So a Windows guest on base=utc needs RealTimeIsUniversal set in its registry, from an admin prompt:
reg add HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\TimeZoneInformation /v RealTimeIsUniversal /t REG_DWORD /d 1 /f
title: A QEMU Windows guest's clock falls behind after host suspend

content:
Put a # comment between backslash-continued lines and the command ends there. The rest of the lines run as new commands.
$ cat c.sh #!/usr/bin/env bash echo one \ # a comment two three $ bash c.sh one c.sh: line 4: two: command not found The continuation joins the comment onto the command line, and # then comments out everything to the end of that line, trailing backslash included. So the chain breaks at the comment. Move the comment above the command instead.
I found this in a long qemu-system-x86_64 invocation, where I had annotated the -cpu flags in place. Because the line began with exec, the truncated command replaced the shell and the leftover flags never ran at all. No error, just a VM missing every argument after the comment.
title: Bash ends a continued command at an inline comment

TL;DR Put the id your caller already holds in the URI. For an integration API that’s the external id the upstream system sent, as long as it’s unique, stable and safe in a path segment. If it can change, put the primary key in the URI and keep the external id for ingestion.
Two ids for one order # Say you’re filling out the CRUD (create, read, update, delete) endpoints on an integration API. Upstream systems push daily snapshots into it, and each record carries an external id: the upstream system’s own id, with its name in front, like crm:ORD-4821. Your database also gives the row a bigint primary key.
So which one goes in /v1/orders/:id?
Ingestion already chose # The ingestion endpoint uses the external id:
PUT /v1/orders/crm:ORD-4821 PUT fits because it’s idempotent: sending the same request twice has the same intended effect as sending it once, and a daily snapshot sends the same record over and over. The upstream system picks the URI, and it only knows the external id.
That leaves the id in the GET, PATCH and DELETE paths, and in the Location header that POST returns. There are three options:
The primary key everywhere, with PUT as the one exception. The external id everywhere. Both, with a second path like /v1/orders/by-external-id/:external_id. Use the caller’s id # A URI identifies a resource, and nothing in HTTP says the id in it has to be your primary key. What matters is which id the caller already holds.
For an integration API the caller is the upstream system, and it holds the external id. With the primary key in the GET, PATCH and DELETE paths, a caller has to get the primary key from a lookup or an earlier response, and store it next to its own id. That’s state the upstream system keeps only because of your URI choice.
scope "/v1", MyAppWeb.API do pipe_through :api post "/orders", OrderController, :create get "/orders/:external_id", OrderController, :show put "/orders/:external_id", OrderController, :upsert patch "/orders/:external_id", OrderController, :update delete "/orders/:external_id", OrderController, :delete end The primary key is still useful to you in logs, support and joins, so return both ids in the body:
# OrderController def create(conn, %{"order" => params}) do {:ok, order} = Orders.create_order(params) conn |> put_status(:created) |> put_resp_header("location", "/v1/orders/#{order.external_id}") |> render(:show, order: order) end # OrderJSON def show(%{order: order}) do %{id: order.id, external_id: order.external_id} end Three tests for the id # The external id has to be:
Unique. The source prefix keeps two sources apart, so crm:ORD-4821 and billing:ORD-4821 are different orders, but each source still has to keep its own ids unique. Drop the prefix and you have a collision the day a second system sends its own ORD-4821. Stable. When an id changes, every client holding the old URI breaks, unless you keep the old one working. Safe in a path segment. RFC 3986 allows the colon in /v1/orders/crm:ORD-4821. A slash isn’t allowed: the caller has to send %2F, and some servers, like Apache, reject that by default. An id that isn’t unique needs a better prefix, whatever goes in the URI. One that isn’t stable means option 1: the primary key goes in the URI, and the external id stays in the ingestion path only. One that isn’t safe in a path can’t go in any path, so ingestion takes it in the body of a POST instead.
The case against both # Option 3 gives one order two URIs, /v1/orders/42 and /v1/orders/by-external-id/crm:ORD-4821. That’s two cache keys for the same row, so every change has to clear both. If you need both, pick one as the address you document and return in Location, and make the other a GET that redirects to it.
title: Which id belongs in the URI

When two Oban jobs GET the same record at once, both get a 404 and both POST it. The second POST gets a 409 Conflict. That 409 means the record exists now, so fetch it again and carry on.
We returned the 409 as an error instead. Oban retried the job until a later GET found the record. The job got there in the end, but each retry reported an error to AppSignal.
The fix matches the conflict right after the create. Request.create/1 is the POST, and request_get/1 is the same GET the job started with:
params |> Request.create() |> case do {:error, [%{"title" => "Conflict"} | _]} -> # another job created it between our GET and POST request_get(params) result -> handle_result(result) end That match takes any 409 Conflict as “already exists”. On an endpoint that can conflict for another reason, match the error detail too.
title: Re-fetch on a 409 when two Oban jobs create the same record

content:
TL;DR If PromEx serves /metrics from your Phoenix endpoint, keep it off the internet with a rule on the load balancer, not an ingress-nginx snippet. A separate metrics port avoids the rule altogether, but needs an app change.
Bramble is a Phoenix LiveView app on Kubernetes, and PromEx feeds its Grafana dashboards. Those metrics are served on the same port as the app, so where do you stop the internet reading them?
PromEx shares the app’s port # PromEx can serve metrics from a plug in the Phoenix endpoint, or from a separate metrics port. We use the plug:
lib/my_app_web/endpoint.ex plug PromEx.Plug, prom_ex_module: MyApp.PromEx config/runtime.exs config :my_app, MyApp.PromEx, # ... metrics_server: :disabled So /metrics answers on the app’s HTTP port (8080 for us), the port every public request reaches. PromEx’s Security Concerns warn against exposing it, and suggest blocking it at “a load balancer or an API gateway”, or guarding the plug itself. We block it in front of the app, and I’ll call that the edge rule.
VictoriaMetrics scrapes 8080 from inside the cluster, so the edge rule never gets in its way.
flowchart TD internet((Internet)) --> edge["edge rule"] edge -->|"all but /metrics"| pod["my-app pod :8080"] scraper["VictoriaMetrics"] -->|"/metrics"| pod A snippet on the ingress # Our first edge rule was an nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/server-snippet annotation, added to every app Ingress by our shared Pulumi helper:
annotations: { "nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/server-snippet": ` location ~* "/metrics" { deny all; return 403; } `, }, That has two problems:
A snippet is raw nginx config, and snippets are the attack vector in CVE-2021-25742: whoever can write an Ingress can read the controller’s secrets. ingress-nginx turned snippet annotations off by default from v1.9.0. To use one now, you turn allow-snippet-annotations back on. You also raise annotations-risk-level, the most dangerous annotation the controller accepts, to Critical. That reopens the hole. It ties the rule to ingress-nginx, which Kubernetes is retiring. Block at the load balancer # We’d already moved the edge rule to our AWS Application Load Balancer, as defence in depth that needed no app change, before the retirement was announced. It answers /metrics with a fixed 403 before the request reaches the cluster.
It matches the path exactly, where the nginx regex matched /metrics anywhere in the path. PromEx.Plug also only answers on the exact path, so /metrics/ or /Metrics gets past the rule and lands on the app’s router instead.
Port or edge rule? # The separate metrics port avoids the edge rule altogether. Drop the plug from the endpoint, give PromEx its own metrics_server, point the scrape at that port, and leave it out of the Service, so no load balancer route leads to it:
config/runtime.exs config :my_app, MyApp.PromEx, # ... metrics_server: [port: 4021, path: "/metrics"] Reach for the edge rule when:
you’d rather not change the app your load balancer already holds the rest of your edge rules Reach for the separate metrics port when:
you can’t be sure every route into the app goes through the same load balancer the people who change the load balancer aren’t the people who add metrics We kept the plug and the edge rule. If I were starting again, I’d try the separate metrics port first, so a new route into the app can’t expose the metrics.
title: Where to block PromEx's /metrics

content:
I recently ran into a simple but frustrating issue with Drata’s Agent for Linux. The agent wouldn’t start, and the logs showed this error:
LaunchProcess: failed to execvp: /opt/Drata [FATAL:zygote_host_impl_linux.cc(201)] Check failed: . : Invalid argument (22) After checking ps to confirm the process wasn’t running and looking through system logs with dmesg and tail -f /var/log/*, I took a closer look at my autostart file:
Exec=/opt/"Drata Agent"/drata-agent The issue? A space in the directory name. While the command worked in the terminal with quotes, the autostart system couldn’t handle it properly and was only executing /opt/Drata.
The fix was straightforward:
sudo mv "Drata Agent" DrataAgent And updating the autostart config:
Exec=/opt/DrataAgent/drata-agent After this change, the agent started without issues. A simple space in a directory name was the culprit all along.
title: A Space Broke the Drata Agent

content:
Imagine this: you’re happily typing away in Neovim, living your best dev life, and suddenly you see an error message like this:
mise ERROR No version is set for shim: node Set a global default version with one of the following: mise use -g node@latest And you think: “But hang on, I do have node = "latest" in my global Mise config (~/.config/mise/config.toml). Did Mise not even read it?”
Well, yes. And, bizarrely, also no. This is the story of how I discovered Mise was effectively giving my global config the silent treatment, while insisting it was “tracked.” Below is the journey, the misdirections that could lead you astray, and the eventual fix that saved my Neovim setup from imploding.
The symptom # In Neovim # LSP and plugins throw “No version is set for shim: node.”
Running :!mise doctor inside Neovim might still show shims_on_path: yes, implying it does find the shims.
However, any configured tools (like Node or Python versions) aren’t actually recognised.
If you run mise doctor in Neovim and see:
ignored_config_files: ~/.config/mise/config.toml …that’s the bright, flashing sign that your global config is effectively in the naughty corner.
In the shell # Initially, your shell appears fine. Possibly from earlier usage or leftover state, you could run Node without hassle. But if you check mise doctor in the shell and see the same “ignored_config_files” line, then yes, Mise is ignoring ~/.config/mise/config.toml there, too. The difference is that your shell had enough leftover “environment sauce” to carry on, while Neovim was left out in the cold. Basically, the shell was “putting on a brave face,” but Neovim was being more candid: no global config, no party.
The red herrings # It’s easy to go down a rabbit hole here. These were my (infuriating) potential culprits along the way.
The missing eval # Mise generally wants you to eval "$(mise init -)" in your ~/.bashrc or ~/.zshrc. If you haven’t done that, heartbreak can follow. But if your shell and Neovim shell commands both report “activated: yes” in mise doctor, then you know this isn’t the problem. Next suspect, please.
Shims outside Neovim’s PATH # It’s common to forget to prepend ~/.local/share/mise/shims to Neovim’s PATH. (The Mise docs mention it, if you RTFM) If that’s missing, you might indeed see “No version is set.” In this situation, though, I’d already done:
local mise_shim_path = vim.fn.expand("~/.local/share/mise/shims") vim.env.PATH = mise_shim_path .. ":" .. vim.env.PATH So the shims were recognised, yet the dreaded “No version is set” still appeared. Therefore, not the culprit.
An invalid config.toml # Sometimes a sneaky “invisible” character or a bung [tools] block can cause issues. But I triple-checked, and it was squeaky clean, with no stray BOM and no dodgy syntax. Another suspect ruled out.
The real culprit # Deep inside Mise’s labyrinthine innards, you’ll find two directories:
~/.local/state/mise/tracked-configs/ ~/.local/state/mise/ignored-configs/ They’re basically two lists of symlinks: one for config files Mise actively loads, and one for config files it’s ignoring. The kicker: if your ~/.config/mise/config.toml somehow appears in both with the same hash, you get Schrödinger’s config, both “tracked” and “ignored,” which effectively means ignored.
My own setup had the same file in both lists:
❯ ls -al ~/.local/state/mise/ignored-configs/ Permissions Size User Date Modified Name lrwxrwxrwx - g 27 Nov 2024 mise-config.toml-506ade9caf4d46ff -> /home/g/.config/mise/config.toml ❯ ls -al ~/.local/state/mise/tracked-configs/ Permissions Size User Date Modified Name lrwxrwxrwx - g 11 Mar 15:16 49bc95cf95659576 -> /home/g/mise-test/.mise.toml lrwxrwxrwx - g 10 Oct 2024 506ade9caf4d46ff -> /home/g/.config/mise/config.toml Notice the exact same hash identifier (506ade9caf4d46ff) appearing in both directories? That’s the smoking gun. My config.toml contained simple version settings:
Why it happens # You might have told Mise to “ignore” that config at some point (maybe after a prompt to trust or not trust the config?), and then later on you or Mise tried to track it again. Now Mise is confused, sees it in both lists, and the “ignore” overrides your “track.” Classic.
Fixing it # Remove the symlink in ignored-configs/.
cd ~/.local/state/mise/ignored-configs ls -l # find something referencing ~/.config/mise/config.toml rm mise-config.toml-<some-hash> Check tracked-configs/. Make sure your config is still there. If it’s missing, Mise may recreate it once you run mise doctor or another command.
Wipe all Mise state, if you want a truly clean slate:
rm -rf ~/.local/state/mise Then re-run mise doctor or mise use -g ... so Mise can rebuild everything.
After that, if you run mise doctor, you should see something like:
shims_on_path: yes config_files: ~/.config/mise/config.toml ignored_config_files: (none) And, finally, Neovim’s LSP or plugins will finally respect your global config’s versions.
Conclusion # If you’re getting “No version is set for shim: node” in Neovim (but not obviously in your shell), don’t be misled by typical PATH or shell init suspects. Check ~/.local/state/mise/ignored-configs/ to see if your global mise config is blacklisted. With that fixed, Neovim’s LSP or plugins will properly recognize the correct binaries.
Quick Recap # Look for your ~/.config/mise/config.toml under ignored-configs/. Remove it if it’s there. Confirm you get shims_on_path: yes for both shell and Neovim. Celebrate having consistent tool versions everywhere! Hopefully that saves you the same confusion I faced. Happy debugging!
title: When Mise Ignores Your Global Config: A Tale of Red Herrings and Stale State

Need to delegate access to your AWS billing dashboard to folks in your finance team? Here’s how you can define read-only billing policies using Pulumi for your Infrastructure As Code (IaC).
First, create an IAM Group:
const group = new aws.iam.Group("finance", { path }); Next, define the policy:
function billingFullPolicy() { const policyDefn: aws.iam.PolicyDocument = { Version: "2012-10-17", Statement: [ { Action: [ "aws-portal:*Billing", "aws-portal:*PaymentMethods", "aws-portal:ViewUsage", "billing:ListBillingViews", "ce:*", "cur:*", "pricing:*", "purchase-orders:*", "support:AddAttachmentsToSet", "support:CreateCase", "sustainability:GetCarbonFootprintSummary", "tax:*", ], Resource: "*", Effect: "Allow", Sid: "FullBillingAndReporting", }, ], }; return new aws.iam.Policy("GrantFullAccessToBilling", { description: `Allow manage billing`, policy: policyDefn, }); } Note this is quite a permissive policy, and you might want to reserve it only for financial ‘administrators’.
A Read-only billing policy might be better suited for reporting users, which might exclude creating Cost and Usage reports (cur:*) or accessing account settings:
function billingReadOnlyPolicy() { const policyDefn: aws.iam.PolicyDocument = { Version: '2012-10-17', Statement: [ { Action: [ 'aws-portal:ViewBilling', 'aws-portal:ViewUsage', 'billing:ListBillingViews', 'ce:GetCostAndUsage' 'cur:DescribeReportDefinitions', 'pricing:*', 'purchase-orders:View*', 'support:AddAttachmentsToSet', 'support:CreateCase', 'sustainability:GetCarbonFootprintSummary', 'tax:Get*', ], Resource: '*', Effect: 'Allow', Sid: 'FullBillingAndReporting', }, { Effect: 'Deny', Action: 'aws-portal:*Account', Resource: '*', Sid: '' } ], } return new aws.iam.Policy('GrantReadAccessToBilling', { description: 'Allow read-only access to billing', policy: policyDefn, }) } Attach the billing policy to the Finance group you created.
new aws.iam.GroupPolicyAttachment("attach-full-billing", { group: group.name, policyArn: billingFullPolicy().arn, }); Now all the IAM users you add to this group will be able to access the these billing permissions.
AWS provides plenty of billing examples, and it’s a simple matter of copying the JSON policy into your Pulumi definitions, using the typescript template above. As an added bonus, if you’re using Typescript, your editor should autoformat the JSON definition for you.
IaC gives you a number of benefits. You have an excellent audit trail, since all policy versions are in a git repository. Your infrastructure is expressed using a familiar, Turing-complete programming language. You manage and deploy code using the same toolchains your DevOps team uses daily.
When you add IaC to your CI/CD pipeline, your cloud infrastructure stays in sync with your definitions. With a tool like Pulumi you also get a web-based dashboard a history of all updates applied to your cloud infrastructure.
(While it sounds like I’m affiliated with Pulumi, I’m not. I am however happy user of their product!)
title: Let Your Finance Team Track AWS Spend

NIST 800-63, section 5 describes the following guidelines for passwords (aka “memorized secrets”):
at least 64 characters, all ASCII (including spaces and Unicode characters) no reusing passwords No password expiration period. No password hints. disallow passwords from data breaches, dictionary or context-specific words, or repetitive or sequential characters Warning: this list excludes several important recommendations like expiry, rate limiting and MFA. NIST now de-emphasizes forcing the use of certain characters (for example uppercase letters, numbers, or special chars like ! @ # $ %) and forcing periodic password rotation. This runs contrary to many password schemes you’ve probably encountered in the wild.
AWS is no exception. Account Password Policies lags these recommendations. There are many (optional) parameters, like requireSymbols, that you can ignore when implementing password schemes for your infrastructure in-line with the latest NIST recommendations.
Here’s what that might look like if you’re using Pulumi to manage your infrastructure definitions:
new aws.iam.AccountPasswordPolicy("nist22-ish", { allowUsersToChangePassword: true, minimumPasswordLength: 64, requireLowercaseCharacters: false, requireNumbers: false, requireSymbols: false, requireUppercaseCharacters: false, passwordReusePrevention: 24, }); The 64 character minimum might seem onerous, but is less of a problem if you use a password manager, or can recite prose from memory /s.
This is just a starting point however. In the same section NIST additionally recommends using second (2FA) or multi-factor (MFA) devices. Start here with some AWS policy definitions you could use to enforce MFA.
title: NIST and AWS Password Policies

Vale.sh is a great tool for enforcing a writing style in your documents.
My vale.sh setup follows the one described in Writing like a pro with vale & Neovim, (albeit with my preferred LunarVim).
Once you’ve got Vale up and running, both it and Neovim spell checking will flag the same things. Technical terms often appear as false positives, so the zg shortcut is handy. (zg adds the word under the cursor as a good word to your spellfile.) However Vale.sh still flags the spelling you just whitelisted:
 Did you really mean 'blargh'? vale (Vale.Spelling) [17, 139] A neat workaround is to link Vale Vocabularies accept.txt to your vim spellfile.
First, set up a Vale Vocab folder
mkdir -p styles/Vocab/Blog/ And configure Vale to use it
diff --git a/.vale.ini b/.vale.ini index 636f9f3..db22387 100644 --- a/.vale.ini +++ b/.vale.ini @@ -4,6 +4,8 @@ MinAlertLevel = suggestion Packages = Microsoft, proselint, Hugo +Vocab = Blog + [*] BasedOnStyles = Vale, Microsoft, proselint Then symlink the Vale accept.txt, for example
% ln -s ~/.config/lvim/spell/en.utf-8.add styles/Vocab/Blog/accept.txt % ll styles/Vocab/Blog/accept.txt lrwxrwxrwx 1 g g 39 Nov 12 17:51 styles/Vocab/Blog/accept.txt -> /home/g/.config/lvim/spell/en.utf-8.add Now if you mark a word as ‘good’ in Neovim, Vale will accept it too.

ERRO[0543] GoError: dial tcp 1.2.3.4:443: socket: too many open files running at go.k6.io/k6/js/modules/k6/ws.(*WS).Connect-fm (native) Indicating a hard limit imposed by the Linux kernel, as the k6 process was trying to establish a lot of simultaneous connections.

Elixir and Phoenix tout high performance with low hardware requirements, and microsecond (μs) response times. Of course Elixir and Phoenix are only one part of your (production) stack, so those numbers only tell you about the application layer.
How well does your Phoenix LiveView app, and infrastructure, perform under stress?
How do you baseline performance, and how do you measure the impact of changes on that performance?
Given LiveView relies on websocket communication, how do you test that? How memory hungry are your views?
I recently had to answer these questions for Bramble which is an app built with Phoenix LiveView. I needed something to simulate HTTP and websocket traffic with spikey and sustained workloads.
Enter k6 # In the past I might have reached for good old Apache JMeter. The new shiny appears to be k6, an open-source load testing tool written by the folks over at Grafana Labs.
My initial impression was good. You write your tests in JavaScript, using a simple API:
import http from "k6/http"; import { sleep } from "k6"; export default function () { http.get("https://test.k6.io"); sleep(1); } k6 ships as a Go binary, optimized for minimal resource consumption. To run a load test, your invoke k6 from the command line:
k6 run --vus 10 --duration 30s script.js This simulates 10 Virtual Users (VUs) over a sustained period of 30 seconds.
You’ll notice k6 is fast. It doesn’t run those tests in a browser or in a NodeJS runtime, but using its own interpreter. This efficiency is important in a load testing tool, as it means you don’t need to rent half of AWS to saturate your application endpoints.
One added benefit, in the context of testing LiveView, is you don’t have to install any extra plugins as websockets are already supported in k6.
Test setup # Here’s a worked example of how to get k6 up and running, and how to test a LiveView app.
The test setup will be simple - we’ll run both a LiveView app, and k6, locally. We’ll write a k6 test script to exercise Chris McCord’s LiveBeats project, described as a “Social Music App With Phoenix LiveView”.
For a production setup, you’ll likely run the tests against a staging or pre-production system instead. Also observe that k6 running locally on a single machine will probably not be good enough for production-like tests. For this use-case, k6 also supports a distributed load test (Kubernetes) or their commercial k6 Cloud.
Install k6 # First, install k6 per their instructions. ASDF users can try asdf-k6.
Set up a LiveView project # Set up your LiveBeats project per the README
(The setup is a little funky as you need to create a GitHub OAuth app for your project, but it only takes 2 minutes).
Open up LiveBeats on localhost, and sign in.
(Optionally create some sample data by uploading a few mp3 files you have lying around on your hard drive. You still have some right? Right?)
LiveBeats has two main URLs we’re interested in for this load test:
The ‘My Profile’ for example /YOUR_GITHUB_USERNAME. The Settings page: /profile/settings A k6 test script # Let’s start our k6 test script, and make it hit just the Settings page first.
test/k6/load-test.js import http from "k6/http"; import { sleep, check } from "k6"; const cookie = __ENV.LIVEBEATS_COOKIE; export default function () { let res = http.get("http://localhost:4000/profile/settings", { // dont follow authentication failure redirects redirects: 0, cookies: { _live_beats_key_v1: cookie, }, }); check(res, { "status 200": (r) => r.status === 200, "contains header": (r) => r.body.includes("Profile Settings"), }); sleep(1); } Source code on GitHub
For simplicity, this script skips GitHub OAuth sign in. Instead it reads a valid cookie from an environment variable.
To do this grab the _live_beats_key_v1 cookie from your browser, and export it in the same session you’ll run k6.
% export LIVEBEATS_COOKIE=YOUR_COOKIE To run this script, use the k6 binary you installed:
% k6 run test/k6/load-test.js /\ |‾‾| /‾‾/ /‾‾/ /\ / \ | |/ / / / / \/ \ | ( / ‾‾\ / \ | |\ \ | (‾) | / __________ \ |__| \__\ \_____/ .io execution: local script: test/k6/load-test.js output: - scenarios: (100.00%) 1 scenario, 1 max VUs, 10m30s max duration (incl. graceful stop): * default: 1 iterations for each of 1 VUs (maxDuration: 10m0s, gracefulStop: 30s) running (00m01.1s), 0/1 VUs, 1 complete and 0 interrupted iterations default ✓ [======================================] 1 VUs 00m01.1s/10m0s 1/1 iters, 1 per VU ✓ status 200 ✓ contains header checks…………………….: 100.00% ✓ 2 ✗ 0 data_received………………: 39 kB 37 kB/s data_sent………………….: 317 B 297 B/s http_req_blocked……………: avg=301.69µs min=301.69µs med=301.69µs max=301.69µs p(90)=301.69µs p(95)=301.69µs http_req_connecting…………: avg=133.67µs min=133.67µs med=133.67µs max=133.67µs p(90)=133.67µs p(95)=133.67µs http_req_duration…………..: avg=63.55ms min=63.55ms med=63.55ms max=63.55ms p(90)=63.55ms p(95)=63.55ms { expected_response:true }…: avg=63.55ms min=63.55ms med=63.55ms max=63.55ms p(90)=63.55ms p(95)=63.55ms http_req_failed…………….: 0.00% ✓ 0 ✗ 1 http_req_receiving………….: avg=208.26µs min=208.26µs med=208.26µs max=208.26µs p(90)=208.26µs p(95)=208.26µs http_req_sending……………: avg=64.63µs min=64.63µs med=64.63µs max=64.63µs p(90)=64.63µs p(95)=64.63µs http_req_tls_handshaking…….: avg=0s min=0s med=0s max=0s p(90)=0s p(95)=0s http_req_waiting……………: avg=63.28ms min=63.28ms med=63.28ms max=63.28ms p(90)=63.28ms p(95)=63.28ms http_reqs………………….: 1 0.938097/s iteration_duration………….: avg=1.06s min=1.06s med=1.06s max=1.06s p(90)=1.06s p(95)=1.06s iterations…………………: 1 0.938097/s vus……………………….: 1 min=1 max=1 vus_max……………………: 1 min=1 max=1 Boom, you can see both checks worked, and the performance statistics for the run. import http from "k6/http"; import { sleep, check } from "k6"; const cookie = __ENV.LIVEBEATS_COOKIE; export default function () { const options = { redirects: 0, cookies: { _live_beats_key_v1: cookie, }, }; let res = http.get("http://localhost:4000/profile/settings", options); check(res, { "status 200": (r) => r.status === 200, "contains header": (r) => r.body.includes("Profile Settings"), }); sleep(1); res = http.get("http://localhost:4000/glennr", options); check(res, { "songs status 200": (r) => r.status === 200, "contains table": (r) => r.body.includes("Artist"), }); sleep(1); } Full diff
Note this is test doesn’t describe a realistic user journey. A sleep time of only 1 second between requests is quite short.
Next, run this updated k6 script with a twist: dial up the VUs + test duration. This increases both the overall the script iterations, and the load on the app.
% k6 run test/k6/load-test.js --vus 100 --duration=10s … running (12.0s), 000/100 VUs, 500 complete and 0 interrupted iterations default ✓ [======================================] 100 VUs 10s ✓ status 200 ✓ contains header ✓ songs status 200 ✓ contains table checks…………………….: 100.00% ✓ 2000 ✗ 0 data_received………………: 62 MB 5.2 MB/s data_sent………………….: 312 kB 26 kB/s http_req_blocked……………: avg=92.64µs min=1.56µs med=4.05µs max=3.53ms p(90)=31.17µs p(95)=346.09µs http_req_connecting…………: avg=34.23µs min=0s med=0s max=2.7ms p(90)=5.74µs p(95)=157.69µs http_req_duration…………..: avg=166.02ms min=55.06ms med=158.57ms max=435.99ms p(90)=274.61ms p(95)=323.83ms { expected_response:true }…: avg=166.02ms min=55.06ms med=158.57ms max=435.99ms p(90)=274.61ms p(95)=323.83ms http_req_failed…………….: 0.00% ✓ 0 ✗ 1000 http_req_receiving………….: avg=155.92µs min=37.41µs med=108.94µs max=2.39ms p(90)=240.32µs p(95)=327.97µs http_req_sending……………: avg=32.7µs min=6.24µs med=17.27µs max=2.71ms p(90)=36.1µs p(95)=100.31µs http_req_tls_handshaking…….: avg=0s min=0s med=0s max=0s p(90)=0s p(95)=0s http_req_waiting……………: avg=165.84ms min=54.96ms med=158.41ms max=435.45ms p(90)=274.34ms p(95)=323.64ms http_reqs………………….: 1000 83.414907/s iteration_duration………….: avg=2.33s min=2.14s med=2.31s max=2.58s p(90)=2.46s p(95)=2.53s iterations…………………: 500 41.707454/s vus……………………….: 1 min=1 max=100 vus_max……………………: 100 min=100 max=100 With the increased Our p90 HTTP request duration has increased to 274ms, and we processed 83 HTTP requests per second.
Try increasing your VU count and observe what happens. I hit my open file descriptor limit at about 1000 VUs. This crashed the phx.server process, and causing all k6 checks to fail. (The BEAM was still running, of course…)
% k6 run test/k6/load-test.js --vus 1000 --duration=10s Websockets and LiveView # A common LiveView optimization for heavy pages is to defer certain costly operations until the view upgrades to a stateful connection.
def mount(params, _session, socket) do %{current_user: current_user} = socket.assigns if connected?(socket) do <do costly things> … As such, any load test that hits these LiveView endpoints purely over HTTP is a lie. To exercise these code paths in a load test, you have to simulate this life cycle by connecting from the client (k6) back to the server over websockets.
As mentioned, k6 supports websockets out of the box. (Note: At time of writing the xk6-websockets extension may replace this API.) Lets add some extra checks to the k6 script to exercise LiveView websockets
import http from "k6/http"; import { sleep, check, fail } from "k6"; import ws from "k6/ws"; const cookie = __ENV.LIVEBEATS_COOKIE; export default function () { const host = "localhost:4000"; const origin = `http://${host}`; const wsProtocol = "ws"; const options = { redirects: 0, cookies: { _live_beats_key_v1: cookie, }, }; let url = `http://${host}/profile/settings`; let res = http.get(url, options); check(res, { "status 200": (r) => r.status === 200, "contains header": (r) => r.body.includes("Profile Settings"), }); checkLiveViewUpgrade(host, origin, wsProtocol, cookie, res, url); sleep(1); url = `http://${host}/glennr`; res = http.get(url, options); check(res, { "songs status 200": (r) => r.status === 200, "contains table": (r) => r.body.includes("Artist"), }); checkLiveViewUpgrade(host, origin, wsProtocol, cookie, res, url); sleep(1); } Where checkLiveViewUpgrade looks like this:
// Connects the websocket to ensure the LV is upgraded. // // - parse the response HTML to find the LiveView websocket connection information (csrf token, topic etc) // - build a `phx_join` message payload // - issue a ws.connect() // - including several callback handlers // - when a socket message was received, we assume the view was upgraded, and the websocket is closed. function checkLiveViewUpgrade( host, testHost, wsProto, cookie, response, url, opts = {} ) { const debug = opts.debug || false; // The response html contains the LV websocket connection details const props = grabLVProps(response); const wsCsrfToken = props.wsCsrfToken; const phxSession = props.phxSession; const phxStatic = props.phxStatic; const topic = `lv:${props.phxId}`; const ws_url = `${wsProto}://${host}/live/websocket?vsn=2.0.0&_csrf_token=${wsCsrfToken}`; if (debug) console.log(`connecting ${ws_url}`); // LV handshake message const joinMsg = JSON.stringify( encodeMsg(null, 0, topic, "phx_join", { url: url, params: { _csrf_token: wsCsrfToken, _mounts: 0, }, session: phxSession, static: phxStatic, }) ); var response = ws.connect( ws_url, { headers: { Cookie: `_live_beats_key_v1=${cookie}`, Origin: testHost, }, }, function (socket) { socket.on("open", () => { socket.send(joinMsg); if (debug) console.log(`websocket open: phx_join topic: ${topic}`); }), socket.on("message", (message) => { checkMessage(message, `"status":"ok"`); socket.close(); }); socket.on("error", handleWsError); socket.on("close", () => { // should we issue a phx_leave here? if (debug) console.log("websocket disconnected"); }); socket.setTimeout(() => { console.log("2 seconds passed, closing the socket"); socket.close(); fail("websocket closed"); }, 2000); } ); checkStatus(response, 101); } Helper functions omitted for brevity, but the source code is here
Note: checkLiveViewUpgrade only tests the websocket connects - it doesn’t test the contents of the websocket message (like if the phx_reply rendered some expected HTML.)
Socket to me # Lets re-run, using the same test parameters as before (100 VUs over 10 seconds)
